speaker_role: young creator/essay reviewer (self-described 20-year-old who has read a couple hundred essays); not an admissions officer
commercial_incentive: Offers paid personalized essay review; also criticizes big consulting firms and counselors as overcharging.
key_insights: Argues the essay matters but is only one part of holistic review, so over-stressing produces stilted writing.
The essay's job is to tell colleges something they cannot get from the activity list, awards or supplements; do not use it as a brag sheet.
Write as a story that engages and shows traits rather than states them, e.g. demonstrate maturity through a scene instead of claiming it.
Brainstorm over a week or more; talk to parents, browse childhood photos, freewrite, and jot ideas in a phone notes file.
Shortlist about three ideas that excite you, then test whether the essay is about you and whether someone else could swap in their name.
End briefly, in two to three sentences, ideally with a callback to the opening, and avoid a zoom-out moral.
specific_numbers_or_facts: Claims some consultancies push packages costing around $10,000 (unsourced, speaker's assertion).
Suggests limiting conclusions to two to three sentences.
notable_or_distinctive: The name-swap uniqueness test and the circular-ending advice are practical, wrapped in an anti-consulting stance.
reliability_notes: Speaker has no admissions-office experience, makes sweeping accusations about the industry, and also sells review services.
